name: Covering the sphere with 50 equal caps
description: Place 50 points on the unit sphere so that the largest angular distance from any point of the sphere to its nearest chosen point (the covering radius) is as small as possible. The best known covering, with radius 18.3000226 degrees, was found by Hardin, Sloane and Smith in 1994 and is not proven optimal.

sources.locator: Tarnai and Gáspár (1991), Covering a sphere by equal circles, and the rigidity of its graph: the covering problem, conjectured coverings for N = 15-20 and sporadic larger N.

Hardin, Sloane and Smith table of coverings by N spherical caps in 3 dimensions (calculations of 1994, maintained by H. Cohn; radii rounded up), row N = 50: 18.3000226 degrees; coordinates in cov3-50.txt (also neilsloane.com/coverings/dim3/cover.3.50.txt).

requirements.datasets: None; the record value is embedded as a parameter and no file is read at evaluation time.

evaluation.benchmark: Covering the sphere with 50 equal caps
evaluation.paper_metric: Local protocol; see candidate contract and source adaptation notes

execution.interface: construct() -> array of shape (N, 3) of nonzero vectors; each is normalised to the unit sphere. Score: the covering radius in degrees, max over points y of the sphere of the angular distance from y to the nearest configuration point (the largest circumradius of the facets of the convex hull, each facet checked to have an empty cap); minimize. Coincident points, configurations inside a closed hemisphere, numerically inconsistent hulls, a wrong shape or non-finite values make the candidate invalid.

limitations: The table gives covering radii rounded up to 1e-7 degrees; a covering counts as a new record only when it is below the table value by more than 1e-7 degrees. Optimal coverings are proven only for small N; the table value for N = 50 dates from 1994, and the value for N = 130 is Henry Cohn's 2026 improvement of the 1994 value.
Points are normalised to the unit sphere before scoring, so only directions matter; the record coordinates are public, so scores measure the returned construction, not the search that produced it.
Candidate Python runs inside the evaluator process and is trusted research code; the evaluator recomputes the score from the returned array but does not sandbox the program.

state_of_the_art.statement: The best known covering of the sphere by 50 equal caps has angular covering radius 18.3000226 degrees (rounded up), from the table of R. H. Hardin, N. J. A. Sloane and W. D. Smith (1994), now maintained by H. Cohn, who invites improvements. No optimality proof is known for N = 50.

science_relevance.scientific_problem: Find 50 points on the sphere whose equal caps of smallest possible angular radius cover the whole sphere.
science_relevance.importance_rationale: Optimal spherical coverings bound the worst-case error of placing sites, sensors or quadrature points on the sphere; they are proven only for small N, and the 1994 records for larger N remain open to improvement.
